[liongalahad] owning the physical disk and all the rituals that come with playing them is a huge deal for many music enthusiasts.
the idea that being analogue they sound somehow objectively better than digital is bull and has been factually disproven. on the other hand the fact that vinyls sound subjectively better than digital for many is true, due to the fuzzy and "warm" feeling they transmit while playing, so for these reasons many prefer them
[AustriaBargain] Nostalgia, or longing for a nostalgia you are too young to have. It's how music was done for a long time and how most of the best albums ever were originally sold and listened to. The sound isn't really the most important part of the experience or else everyone would listen to professional vinyl rips. It's the weight of the album in your hand, the huge artwork you can study, physically seeing the gaps between songs when you want to choose a certain song, knowing that's how your father and grandfather and grandfather listened to music their whole lives. If you have no interest in vinyl as a cultural artefact then Spotify or Apple Music is much better value.
[DustyAfternoon] It’s commodity fetishisation. And I say that as a guy with a nascent vinyl collection.
Adding an album on Spotify? Yeah ok. You can listen to it, but it’s not yours . It can be removed at any time. Anyone else can click ‘add’ too. There’s no physical presence. There’s no emotional or financial weight to it.
A vinyl? That’s yours . It says ‘I like this enough to spend money to have it physically’.
It’s also a cool mechanism. Vinyl is on the precipice of where technology goes from physical to magical. At the very least, it’s a grown up fidget spinner.
I didn’t get it until I saw someone else’s collection. Then I got it.
[fishnchipsncoke] It's nice to actually process things you like. Not have a picture on a screen. It's very enjoyable just like anything you enjoy to actually interact with it. Great album art, sometimes cool booklets and discs, your actually actively listening to music, choosing an album that you actually decide to listen through. Not just shuffle a bunch of hits.
Giving back to an artist that's given you hundreds or thousands of hours of pleasure.

[krammis76] Quick question for the vinyl people here. Is cleaning them regularly a good plan? And what sort of cleaning kit is good for beginners. I often see some good titles at my local op shops but I'm guessing they'll be a bit dirty most of the time. Any tips for a beginner?
[justtoreply] Cleaning what? The vinyl, surely not. Just like discs I presume it scratches like buggery. The burger? Maybe.
[krammis76] Yeah the vinyl. I'm guessing playing one with dirt on it will probably mess up the needle eventually.
[zbzylg] No need to clean it regularly but make sure you clean it thoroughly with things like spin-cleaner before first play cuz even brand-new vinyls can be(visibly) pretty dirty.
Afterwards just quickly do a sweeping with something like an anti-static brush before lowering arm.
Depending on your inner bag the situation can also be different. HDPE is usually cleaner than paper which has a larger chance of generating fragments.
In short:
Spin cleaner for first cleaning, anti-static brush for brief cleaning before replay and HDPE inner bag for storage.
[clandestino] If you've bought a 2nd hand LP that's dirty (or maybe just one of your existing records has some dirt/grime on it) - just fill a plastic tub with warm water and a tiny drop of washing up liquid. Clean the LP with a soaking wet microfiber cloth, then dry with another cloth…and let it air - dry for a few minutes.
The above might appear crazy at first glance… But give it a try, you'll be very surprised at the difference it makes!!
Edit - if you're sceptical about the above… Then buy two old, dirty 2nd hand LPs. Play them both for a few minutes to listen to the crackles…. Record the audio on your phone. Then clean one with an electro static cleaner, the other with warm water + drop of detergent. Then simply play the records again and listen.
[krammis76] @clandestino: Thanks for the info guys. Basic and cheap cleaning is what I was looking for. Appreciate it. Looking forward to grabbing the unit this morning and start the hunt for cheap vinyls. :)
[NBSales] I just cleaned about 1500 records recently with an electrostatic cleaner and it took such a long time. These were 50+ years old full of grime, smoke, dust etc. On new records don't bother. Just get a brush for fluff prior to playing. Cleaning new records is a bit gimmicky IMHO as they won't have the dust, oils, smoke etc.
